metadata.title: How a student’s month of birth is linked to performance at school (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses PISA 2018 microdata to relate students’ month of birth (via relative age within the school-entry cohort) to cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes. PISA is collected using a complex, multi-stage sampling design (students nested in schools, with stratification and clustering), so analyses should use the PISA sampling weights provided in the PISA database to obtain population-representative estimates. The document does not report specific weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures, so the safest practice is to apply the standard PISA student weights and, where available, replicate weights for variance estimation. Because the study is not framed as an ML prediction pipeline, it should follow PISA/OECD best practices for handling plausible values for achievement outcomes and for computing standard errors under the complex design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports associations and estimated effects using PISA outcomes (including reading, mathematics, science and several non-cognitive indices), but it does not document a plausible-values strategy (e.g., Rubin’s rules across PVs) or any explicit missing-data procedure. This is a reporting gap for a study that relies on PISA achievement measures, which are typically PV-based. The absence of documented PV/missing-data handling prevents assessing how uncertainty from imputation/estimation was propagated into the reported cross-country estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PISA 2018 student data for students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months, enrolled at grade 7 or higher. It further restricts analyses to countries/economies with available information on school-entry regulations (cut-off dates and first day of the school year) and, for some outcomes, to subsets where relevant contextual variables are available (e.g., reported age at school entry, grade repetition in primary school, self-concept/self-efficacy indices, bullying exposure). For the section on advancing/delaying entry, it excludes Colombia from the analyses because it is not possible to distinguish students located in regions with different cut-off dates. For some figures/estimates, it also distinguishes systems where the PISA sample spans one versus two grade cohorts, and it uses theoretical grade controls derived from regulations rather than actual enrolled grade to reduce selection bias.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2018 to study how month of birth relates to students’ relative age within their school-entry cohort and, in turn, to cognitive outcomes (reading, mathematics, science) and multiple non-cognitive outcomes (self-perceived competence and difficulty in reading, self-efficacy and fear of failure, motivation/attitudes toward competition, expectations to complete tertiary education, and bullying exposure). It also documents how school-entry regulations (cut-off dates and school-year start dates) vary across more than 45 participating countries/economies and how strictly they are applied, using contextual questionnaire information on students’ age at entry. The paper reports that being among the youngest in the grade cohort is associated with lower performance across PISA domains and with higher likelihood of repeating a grade in primary school, and in several systems with lower self-confidence and weaker future education expectations. It emphasizes that disentangling age-at-test, age-at-entry, and schooling duration is difficult and that identification relies on theoretical relative age derived from regulations, with caution about cross-country comparability and selection effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper/report that synthesizes and analyzes PISA 2018 outcomes using policy-relevant constructs (relative age, grade repetition, socio-emotional indices) rather than training or evaluating machine-learning predictive models. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract and no ML-style target-variable performance metrics to tabulate. The paper also does not provide enough methodological detail in the excerpt to extract PV-combining rules or missing-data handling, so those fields are treated as not reported.
